issues.legal_issue: A registration authority may register a unilateral cancellation deed when no applicable rule requires the consent or participation of the parties to the earlier conveyance.
material_facts: A society had executed a deed purporting to extinguish an earlier registered sale deed and presented it for registration without the participation of the earlier purchaser or the purchaser’s successors.
The dispute arose in a state where no rule comparable to the rule discussed in the judgment required the parties to the earlier conveyance to execute or consent to a cancellation deed.
The appellant asked registration authorities to cancel the registration, and the dispute reached the Court in an appeal from the dismissal of a writ petition.
issues.conclusion: Justice Dipak Misra expressed the view that, absent a specific rule requiring the earlier parties’ participation, the registration authority could not refuse to register a cancellation deed solely because those parties were absent or had not consented. He considered the general observations in Thota Ganga Laxmi to require consideration by a larger Bench. The judges disagreed, and the matter was referred to the Chief Justice for constitution of a larger Bench; this proposition was therefore not resolved by a majority holding in this judgment.
issues.legal_principle: The Registration Act, 1908, including Sections 17, 20, 21, 32, 34 and 69, gives registration officers administrative functions and does not confer general authority to adjudicate title or disputed questions. Section 69 empowers the Inspector-General to make rules consistent with the Act. Justice Dipak Misra distinguished the Andhra Pradesh rule considered in Thota Ganga Laxmi v. Government of Andhra Pradesh, (2010) 15 SCC 207, and discussed Yanala Malleshwari v. Anantula Sayamma, AIR 2007 AP 57, E.R. Kalaivan v. Inspector General of Registration, AIR 2010 Madras 18, and M. Ramakrishna Reddy v. Sub Registrar, AIR 2000 Karnataka 46.

rule.if: registration_challenge_proceeding and cancellation_deed_presented and no_applicable_rule_requires_prior_party_consent and registration_requirements_met

predicates.registration_challenge_proceeding: A party challenges a registration authority’s handling of a document in a proceeding concerning registration.
predicates.cancellation_deed_presented: A document purporting to cancel or extinguish an earlier registered conveyance is presented for registration.
predicates.no_applicable_rule_requires_prior_party_: No applicable rule requires the parties to the earlier conveyance to execute or consent to the cancellation document.
predicates.registration_requirements_met: The presented document satisfies the applicable requirements for registration.

issues.definition: When a cancellation document is presented in a registration challenge, the registration requirements are met, and no applicable rule requires the earlier parties’ consent, the registrar cannot refuse registration solely for lack of that consent.

issues.legal_issue: A writ court may decline to adjudicate the validity of registered property documents when a competent statutory forum is already considering the underlying dispute and the circumstances include a compromise payment.
material_facts: The appellant’s challenge to the society’s cancellation of the earlier allotment and the resulting property dispute was pending before the competent cooperative authority.
The appellant had entered into a compromise with a subsequent purchaser and received consideration, while continuing to pursue proceedings concerning the property.
The appellant sought, in a writ petition, a declaration that the registered documents were void and directions to the registration authorities to record their cancellation.
The High Court declined to decide the documents’ validity in the writ proceeding and directed the appellant to pursue the matter before an appropriate forum.
issues.conclusion: Justice Dipak Misra concluded that the High Court had correctly declined to decide the dispute in the writ proceeding because the competent statutory forum was considering the underlying dispute and the appellant had received compromise consideration. The other judge dissented on the availability of writ relief. Because of that disagreement, the judgment did not produce a majority resolution of the issue.
issues.legal_principle: Justice Dipak Misra relied on the distinction between the administrative registration function and adjudication of disputed rights, and on the pending proceeding before the competent authority under the M.P. Cooperative Societies Act, 1960. He referred to Thota Ganga Laxmi v. Government of Andhra Pradesh, (2010) 15 SCC 207, and to the earlier order concerning the request for appointment of a receiver, which noted the pending dispute, possession, and the compromise payment.

predicates.writ_challenge_to_registered_documents: A person asks a writ court to declare registered property documents invalid or to direct their cancellation.
predicates.underlying_dispute_pending_before_compet: A competent statutory forum is already considering the underlying dispute about the property or the authority for the transaction.
predicates.compromise_consideration_received: The person challenging the documents has received consideration under a compromise concerning the dispute.

issues.definition: If a writ challenge concerns registered property documents, the underlying dispute is pending before a competent forum, and the challenger has received compromise consideration, the writ court may decline to adjudicate the documents’ validity.

issues.legal_issue: A unilateral cancellation of an absolute registered conveyance, followed by transfers based on that cancellation, is invalid when the cancellation is not supported by the affected parties’ consent or an order of a competent court.
material_facts: A society had executed and registered an absolute sale deed in favour of the appellant’s mother, who later died leaving the appellant and his sister as successors.
The society later executed a cancellation or extinguishment deed unilaterally, relying on its bye-laws, and subsequent sale deeds were made in reliance on that deed.
The appellant challenged the cancellation and the subsequent transfers, asserting that they impaired rights acquired under the earlier registered conveyance.
Justice V. Gopala Gowda treated the material facts as undisputed and considered the cancellation and later transfers to be unsupported by consent or a competent court order.
issues.conclusion: In dissent, Justice V. Gopala Gowda would have held the unilateral extinguishment deed and the subsequent sale deeds void, set them aside, and granted relief to the appellant. Justice Dipak Misra did not agree that the appeal should be allowed on that basis, and the judges referred the matter to a larger Bench; the proposed ruling was therefore not a majority holding of the Court.
issues.legal_principle: Justice V. Gopala Gowda relied on Section 31 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, under which a court may adjudge an instrument void or voidable and, where it is registered, communicate its cancellation to the registering officer; Section 62 of the Contract Act, 1872, concerning rescission or alteration by agreement; Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882; Article 59 of the Limitation Act, 1963; and Article 300A of the Constitution. He relied on Thota Ganga Laxmi v. Government of Andhra Pradesh, (2010) 15 SCC 207, E.R. Kalaivan v. Inspector General of Registration, AIR 2010 Madras 18, and Pratap Singh v. State of Punjab, AIR 1964 SC 72. He also considered the principles governing writ relief in CAG v. K.S. Jagannathan, (1986) 2 SCC 679; Andi Mukta Sadguru v. V.R. Rudani, (1989) 2 SCC 691; and Hari Vishnu Kamath v. Ahmad Ishaque, AIR 1955 SC 233.

rule.if: appeal_from_writ_denial and prior_absolute_registered_conveyance and cancellation_unilateral and no_affected_party_consent and no_competent_court_order and later_transfers_rely_on_cancellation

predicates.appeal_from_writ_denial: A party appeals after a writ court has denied relief concerning disputed property documents.
predicates.prior_absolute_registered_conveyance: An earlier absolute conveyance of the property was registered in favour of the person whose rights are later challenged.
predicates.cancellation_unilateral: The original transferor or another party purports to cancel the earlier conveyance without the participation of the affected parties.
predicates.no_affected_party_consent: The affected parties have not agreed to rescind or cancel the earlier conveyance.
predicates.no_competent_court_order: No competent court has ordered the cancellation of the earlier conveyance.
predicates.later_transfers_rely_on_cancellation: Later conveyances were made on the basis of the purported cancellation.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges the denial of writ relief, an earlier absolute registered conveyance is cancelled unilaterally without affected-party consent or a competent court order, and later transfers rely on that cancellation, the cancellation and dependent transfers are void.

issues.legal_issue: A compromise relied on to oppose relief concerning disputed property does not bar that relief when the agreement has been rescinded and the consideration has been demanded back.
material_facts: The appellant entered into a compromise concerning the property and received consideration from a subsequent purchaser.
After the appellant pursued further proceedings, the purchaser’s lawyer sent a notice demanding repayment of the consideration and asserting that the appellant had violated the compromise.
Justice V. Gopala Gowda treated the notice as rescinding the agreement and concluded that it could not be relied on to deny the appellant relief.
issues.conclusion: In dissent, Justice V. Gopala Gowda concluded that the compromise did not bar relief because the agreement had been rescinded and repayment had been demanded. Justice Dipak Misra relied in part on the receipt of compromise consideration when concluding that the writ court had properly declined to intervene. The judges disagreed, so the judgment did not establish a majority ruling on the effect of the compromise.
issues.legal_principle: Justice V. Gopala Gowda relied on Section 62 of the Contract Act, 1872, concerning rescission or alteration of contracts, and on the notice demanding return of the consideration as evidence that the compromise had been rescinded. He also considered that the compromise was made while proceedings concerning the property were pending.

predicates.property_dispute_proceeding: A proceeding concerns a dispute over rights in property.
predicates.compromise_used_to_oppose_relief: A party relies on a compromise to argue that the opposing party should not receive relief.
predicates.repayment_demanded_after_further_proceed: After further proceedings are pursued, a party demands repayment of the consideration paid under the compromise.

issues.definition: When a compromise is relied on to oppose relief in a property dispute but repayment is demanded after further proceedings, the rescinded compromise does not bar that relief.
